content:
Nuevo Laredo just passed a milestone that won’t make anyone’s campaign mailer — 5,122 trees planted across the city under the municipal reforestation program “Arboleando NLD.” It is the kind of quiet civic work that compounds: more shade, cooler streets, cleaner air, and a greener border for the neighborhoods that need it most.

Tania Taboada Blanco, the city’s general coordinator of Environmental Management, reported the numbers this week. Between September and October 15, 2026, crews planted 464 trees in the program’s second reforestation period of the year, bringing the 2026 total to 1,872. The administration-wide tally for 2024–2027 now stands at 5,122 trees, under the municipal government headed by Mayor Carmen Lilia Canturosas Villarreal.

“En esta administración que encabeza nuestra presidenta Carmen Lilia Canturosas Villarreal, que es del 2024 a lo que va del 2026, traemos una cifra en reforestación de 5 mil 122 árboles reforestados a la fecha,” Taboada Blanco said.

Native trees, planned where they matter

The program does not plant randomly. Taboada Blanco said plantings are organized around medians, plazas, and public spaces, plus requests from residents — a way to spread vegetation into different sectors of the city. Just as important is what gets planted: native species that can take Nuevo Laredo’s heat and, once established, need less water than non-native alternatives. Among them: mesquite, anacahuita, encino (oak), crespón, and palo blanco. The mesquite, she noted, also supports pollinators — a small ecological win on top of the shade.

She emphasized that planting is only half the job: choosing the right species for local conditions and following up on their adaptation is what makes the trees survive and thrive, particularly in a region where water scarcity is a constant reality.

Free help for residents who want to plant

Taboada Blanco invited residents to ask for guidance before planting, pruning, or removing a tree — to check the space and the permits required. Her department also offers free environmental education activities: germination workshops, school and urban gardens, composting, and reforestation events.

Border cities on both sides of the Rio Grande run hot, dry, and dusty. A tree is never just a tree here — it is a shade canopy for a bus stop, a cooler schoolyard, a small buffer against the dust that sweeps through both Laredos. Five thousand of them is a start worth celebrating, and a reminder that the unglamorous work of city government — planning, species selection, follow-up — is what makes the green last.
